judge_assessment.explanation: The judge's arithmetic is exact. I re-solved every item and independently counted the drawn models: problem 1's array is 4 rows of 5 tiles (4 x 5 = 20, missing factor 5), problem 2 shows three equal bags of six dots (3 x 6 = 18, missing factor 6), problem 3's seating chart is 4 rows of 7 (28 / 7 = 4). The rest give 7, 7, 7, 5, 9, 9 and problem 10's pair 8 and 7 — the judge's list exactly, and each figure matches its verify entry. Units are handled well: 'chairs' and 'packs' are declared as answer_unit and printed on both the worksheet answer line and the key's boxed answer. My disagreement is with instruction_following at 4/4. The prompt's closing sentence is 'Verify every machine-checkable answer and clearly label any genuinely open response for manual review', and two of the ten problems demand written prose: problem 9, 'Explain in one sentence what Mia did instead of finding a missing factor, then write the correct missing factor', and problem 10, 'Write both missing-factor equations, then explain in one sentence why the number in each row got smaller when the number of rows got bigger.' verify.json contains no {"type": "manual"} entry (machine_observation: gate_chain_manual_flags false), and final_response.md closes with 'Nothing is flagged for manual review — the build finished all green with no unverified items', which is not true of the sentence a child is asked to write twice. The answer key does model both explanations in prose ('What Mia did was subtract', 'Why it flips'), which is why this is a contract defect rather than a grading failure — but the delivery text tells the parent there is nothing to read, and there is.

strengths_to_preserve: The unit binding is complete in both directions on the two story problems that carry one: verify.json ids 6 and 7 declare answer_unit 'chairs' and 'packs', the worksheet answer lines print 'Answer: ____ chairs' and 'Answer: ____ packs', and the key boxes '7 chairs' and '5 packs'. The key even teaches why: 'the unit belongs in the answer. "Seven" alone does not say seven of what.'

Problem 10 splits one context into two bound checks — 7 x [box] = 56 giving 8, then 8 x [box] = 56 giving 7 — so the reciprocal structure the item is about is machine-proved rather than asserted, and the key closes with 'the total never changed, so more rows must mean fewer counters in each row'.

The three declared traps are all the same misconception (subtract instead of divide) landing on three distinct values — 63 - 9 = 54, 72 - 8 = 64, 36 - 4 = 32 — so a grader seeing any of them knows precisely what happened; the key prints them under 'Common wrong answers'.

The facet ramp is honest: three picture-grounded missing factors (1-3), three bare number sentences (4, 5, 8), two unit-carrying stories (6, 7), then error analysis and a two-part reciprocal item, so the same equation type is met in four different clothes without an identical skeleton.

The study guide's three sections match the three worksheet facets one-for-one, each with a rule ('a missing factor is found by dividing. Total / known factor = missing factor'), a worked example, and a re-parameterised try-it, plus a watch-out naming the exact trap the worksheet plants.

root_causes.description: Items whose stem explicitly asks the student to 'explain in one sentence' are recorded as ordinary machine-verified entries, with no manual companion, so the gate chain reports zero items requiring a human read and the delivery text repeats that claim. SKILL.md already reserves 'manual' for explanation answers (line 249, line 257), but no gate detects the mismatch between an explanation stem and a purely numeric verify record.
evidence: worksheet.pdf problem 9: 'Explain in one sentence what Mia did instead of finding a missing factor, then write the correct missing factor.' verify.json id 9 is a single {"type": "eval", "expr": "p/q", "at": {"p": 36, "q": 4}, "expected": 9} entry.

worksheet.pdf problem 10: '... then explain in one sentence why the number in each row got smaller when the number of rows got bigger.' verify.json id 10 holds two 'solve' entries (8 and 7) and nothing for the explanation.
verify.json contains no entry with "type": "manual"; machine_observation records gate_chain_manual_flags: false and unique_verified_problems 10 of 10.
final_response.md: 'Nothing is flagged for manual review — the build finished all green with no unverified items.'

improvements.title: Require a manual companion entry when a worksheet stem asks the student to explain
improvements.proposed_change: Add an open-response scan to tests/check_answer_line.py, which already receives both the worksheet .tex and verify.json and already runs as build.sh gate 10. Segment with _tex_segments.segment_spans; for each problem region match a closed lexicon of explanation cues ('explain', 'why', 'in your own words', 'say how you know', 'what do you notice', 'describe', 'draw', 'circle') and exit 1 when the matching id has no {"type": "manual"} entry, printing the problem number, the matched phrase and the JSON line to add. For curr-078 the fix is two entries: id 9 gains a manual entry whose desc is the model the key already prints ('a full-credit answer says Mia subtracted 4 from 36 instead of splitting 36 into 4 equal groups'), and id 10 gains one for the inverse-relationship sentence. The build then exits 2 with two manual items and the final response says so.
improvements.regression_test: Add tests/fixtures/explain_stem_unflagged/ with a worksheet whose problem 1 reads 'Explain in one sentence what Mia did instead of finding a missing factor, then write the correct missing factor.' and a verify.json whose id 1 holds only {"type": "eval", "expr": "p/q", "at": {"p": 36, "q": 4}, "expected": 9}. Assert check_answer_line.py exits 1 and names problem 1 and 'Explain'. Append {"id": 1, "type": "manual", "desc": "..."} and assert the same call exits 0.
improvements.expected_impact: Removes the false all-green claim on this case and on the 36-case cluster behind the key. The grader is told that two sentences on this sheet are theirs to read and is handed the acceptance criteria; the answer key content does not change, since it already models both explanations.
improvements.risk: A prose lexicon will occasionally fire on an incidental 'why' inside a teaching note. Scan only the student-facing stem (comments blanked), keep the lexicon closed and versioned like tests/_units.py, and make the failure message a copy-pasteable JSON fix so a genuine false positive costs an author one line.

case_summary: A precise missing-factor set with correct answers throughout — I re-solved all eleven checks and re-counted every drawn model (4 rows of 5, three bags of six, 4 rows of 7 seats), and each figure agrees with its verify entry and with the key. The design earns its marks: three ways into the same equation (picture, bare sentence, story), units declared and bound on both the sheet line and the key box for the two story problems that carry them, three traps that all encode 'subtract instead of divide' at three distinguishable values, and problem 10's reciprocal pair verified as two separate checks. The single defect is the verification contract. Problems 9 and 10 each end with 'explain in one sentence', which is precisely what SKILL.md reserves the manual type for, yet neither carries a manual entry; the build finished with zero manual flags and final_response.md told the parent that nothing was left unverified. Because the answer key already prints a model answer for both explanations, the remedy is two JSON entries and a gate that would have refused the build without them — no printed content needs to change.
